mcqs.question: A single call to fork() has just returned in your program. How do you determine whether you're now executing in the parent or the child?
options: You can't distinguish them — both run identical code from that point on
Check whether getpid() returns an even or odd number
Check the return value: 0 means you're in the child, a positive number (the child's PID) means you're in the parent
The child always runs first, so check a global counter
mcqs.explanation: fork()'s return value is the only reliable signal: 0 in the child, the child's PID (a positive number) in the parent, and negative on failure with no child created. There's no ordering or parity guarantee — that's exactly why the return-value check exists.

mcqs.question: In a C program that calls fork() once and then has an if/else printing from each branch, how many total print statements execute across all processes, and why?
options: Two — the fork() call causes execution to continue in both the parent and the child, each hitting a different branch
One — only the child continues past fork()
One — only the parent continues past fork()
Zero — fork() replaces the running code entirely, like exec()
mcqs.explanation: Unlike exec(), fork() doesn't replace code — it clones the process, and both the parent and child continue executing from right after the fork() call, each seeing a different return value and thus taking a different if/else branch. That's two processes, two print statements.

mcqs.question: Why does a shell need fork() and exec() to be separate calls in order to implement `ls > out.txt`?
options: exec() alone can already redirect file descriptors given the right flags
It doesn't — output redirection is handled entirely by the terminal, not the shell
fork() is required twice, once for the redirection and once for the command
The gap between fork() and exec() gives the child a chance to redirect its stdout to the file before exec() loads ls, without affecting the parent shell
mcqs.explanation: The child process, after forking but before exec-ing, can freely modify its own file descriptors (redirecting stdout to a file) without touching the parent shell's descriptors. If fork and exec were one atomic call, there would be no window to do this setup. Redirection is a shell/kernel mechanism, not a terminal one.

mcqs.question: What is a zombie process, precisely?
options: A process that has exited and called exit(), but whose parent hasn't yet called wait() to collect its exit status
A process that is stuck in an infinite loop consuming CPU
A process whose parent died before it did
A process that has been forcibly killed but refuses to terminate
mcqs.explanation: A zombie has already exited — its code, memory, and file descriptors are freed — but the kernel keeps a minimal record until the parent retrieves the exit status via wait(). A process whose parent died first is an orphan, a different concept; a zombie is not stuck or CPU-consuming.

mcqs.question: A process with 4GB of resident memory calls fork(), and the child immediately calls exec() to run a small unrelated program. With copy-on-write, roughly how much of that 4GB actually gets copied?
options: All 4GB, copied eagerly the instant fork() is called
None of it is copied physically at fork time, and since the child overwrites its own address space via exec() almost immediately, essentially no copy-on-write faults occur either
Exactly half, split evenly between parent and child
4GB copied lazily, one page at a time, until the child exits
mcqs.explanation: Copy-on-write means fork() only shares read-only page-table mappings, doing no physical copying at fork time. Because the child calls exec() almost immediately, it never writes to the parent's inherited pages — exec() replaces the address space outright — so the lazy per-page copy mechanism barely triggers at all in this case.

mcqs.question: A long-running server forks a new worker process per incoming request but never calls wait() or waitpid() for them. What eventually happens?
options: Eventually available PIDs are exhausted because exited-but-unreaped children hold PID slots indefinitely, and fork() starts failing system-wide
Nothing — zombies use no memory or CPU, so this is harmless indefinitely
The kernel automatically reaps children after a fixed timeout, so this self-heals
Each worker's memory leaks until the machine runs out of RAM
mcqs.explanation: Zombies are cheap individually but each holds a finite PID slot; never reaping them lets the count grow until PID space is exhausted, breaking fork() for every process on the machine, not just the buggy one. There's no automatic timeout-based reaping, and the issue is PID exhaustion, not a memory leak.
